title: 1-bit full adder
goal: A reader can trace every signal from input to output without guessing where a line goes.

rubric.must: No connecting line passes through the inside of a gate symbol. Lines may touch a gate only at its pins.
Every input and output label is joined to a gate by a visible unbroken line. No signal is connected only by sharing a name.
A filled dot appears exactly where one line branches into two, and nowhere else.
Where two unrelated lines cross, it is visually clear they are not connected (a hop, a gap, or no dot).
Each output label sits on the same horizontal line as the gate pin that drives it.
No two pieces of text overlap, and no text is crossed by a line.

ideal.notes: Gate-level 1-bit full adder in ANSI/IEEE Std 91 distinctive-shape symbols. Inputs A, B and Cin enter as labelled stubs on the left. A and B drive an exclusive-OR whose output is the half-sum net s1, and an AND whose output is the carry-generate net c1. A second exclusive-OR adds Cin to s1 to give Sum; a second AND combines s1 with Cin to give the carry-propagate net c2; an OR gate sums c1 and c2 into Cout. All wires are orthogonal, filled dots mark fan-out junctions, and the two outputs leave on the right margin. Drawn in the idiom of the logic exemplar: ANSI/IEEE Std 91 distinctive shapes on one body box so the columns line up, ink-only palette with paper-filled gate bodies so a wire passing behind a gate is visibly interrupted, the gate type carried by the outline rather than printed under it, and the label slot spent on net names instead. Row pitch, channel x and canvas size are solved from browser-measured text widths, and the drawing was checked label-against-label, label-against-wire, label-against-canvas-edge and wire-against-every-unattached-gate before it was written: 0 collisions, and no wire crosses a gate body.

audit.reviewedBy: a digital design engineer checking a gate-level schematic
